"Fifth time," Dolma muttered, gripping the queue token. "Fifth time for one stamp."

"Deep breath," Anirban said. "Shouting at the counter won't get it stamped."

"I want to. I really want to."

At the window the clerk said, "The file is with the section officer. Come next week."

Dolma's jaw tightened, then loosened. "Thank you. Could I speak to your supervisor, please? I'd like to know who holds the file now."

The clerk sighed and pointed to a door. "Room 4. The supervisor may be in."

Outside the door Anirban said, "Take photos of the token and the receipt."

"Already did. I'll post it on the grievance portal tonight."

"You stayed polite in there."

"The clerk didn't design this system. I'm still tired."

qa.q: How many visits has Dolma made for the same stamp?
qa.a: This is Dolma's fifth visit for one stamp.

qa.q: What is Dolma feeling at the counter, and what shows it is being held back?
qa.a: Dolma is angry and tired; the jaw that tightens and then loosens, and the polite request for the supervisor, show the anger being held back.

qa.q: What could Dolma do if the file still doesn't move?
qa.a: Keep the photos of the token and receipt as a paper trail, ask the supervisor politely who holds the file, and post the complaint on the grievance portal.

qa.q: How might the clerk see Dolma's visit?
qa.a: The clerk may see one more frustrated person in a system the clerk did not design, and may have little say over a file sitting with the section officer.

grounding: After repeated visits Dolma wants to shout at the clerk but breathes, asks for the supervisor politely and keeps a paper trail.

The queue at the town hall in Utrecht was short, but Mina's stomach was tight. She held a folder with her passport, a rental contract and a form she only half understood. At the desk the caseworker, Freya, read everything without a sigh.

"Let's go step by step," Freya said, drawing three boxes on a notepad. "First the address registration, then the stamp, then the card."

One page of the rental contract was missing. Freya phoned the landlord's agent from the desk. Mina hesitated. "Could you leave out the missing page and just approve it?"

Freya smiled. "I can't skip that one, but I can mark your file as urgent."

Mina nodded, feeling a little silly for asking. Two days later the message came: approved. She sent Freya a thank-you card.

qa.q: What three steps did Freya draw on the notepad?
qa.a: Freya drew three boxes: first the address registration, then the stamp, then the card.

qa.q: How did Mina feel after asking Freya to approve the file without the missing page?
qa.a: Mina felt a little silly for asking, which suggests Mina saw it as a request to bend the rules.

qa.q: What could Mina do next time to make things smoother?
qa.a: Bring a complete set of documents, including every page of the rental contract, and keep thanking helpful staff.

qa.q: How might Freya see Mina's request to skip the page?
qa.a: Freya likely sees it as an understandable worry and answers kindly, explaining that the page cannot be skipped while offering what can be done, marking the file as urgent.

grounding: An official patiently explains steps and speeds Mina's file; Mina is prepared and thankful and accepts that kindness does not mean bending rules.

passage:
Dear Joseph,

You'll laugh, but I finally went to the electricity office about the meter shift. The clerk said the file could take months, then lowered a voice and murmured that "a little something" would move it by evening. The only way, apparently. My hand actually went to my purse.

Then I remembered what you once said, that small bribes are practical today and keep alive a system that will let you down tomorrow. So I said, "I'll wait, thank you. Could I meet the section head?" The clerk shrugged. The section head checked the file and said it would be cleared in a few days. I've also put in a request through the online portal and sent an RTI asking about the delay.

It moved without money, though slower, and I'm still irritated. Wish me patience.

Anjali

qa.q: What did the clerk say would move the file by evening?
qa.a: The clerk murmured that "a little something" would move it by evening.

qa.q: Why did Anjali's hand go to the purse, and what made it stop?
qa.a: The wish to get the file moving made Anjali's hand go to the purse, but remembering Joseph's remark that small bribes keep alive a system that lets people down stopped it.

qa.q: What could Anjali do if the file stalls again?
qa.a: Follow up with the section head, check the online portal request, and use the RTI to ask for reasons for the delay.

qa.q: How might the clerk see Anjali's refusal?
qa.a: The clerk may find it unusual, since asking for "a little something" was presented as the only way, though Anjali stayed polite and simply moved to the section head.

grounding: Speed money is offered as the only way; Anjali recognises the ask, declines politely and escalates to the section head and the portal.

passage:
Subject: Still here, still queuing

Hi Aditi,

Four visits to the tehsil office now. Each time a different missing form. Yesterday my token number was 212, and I honestly felt like a number instead of a person 😅 I nearly told myself nothing ever works here and stopped trying.

But that thinking only lets the system off the hook. So I wrote the whole process, forms, counters, timings, on one page and dropped it in our neighbourhood group. Two neighbours used it and finished in one visit each. I am also going to sign the petition for an online tracking system.

Come with me on Sunday to the citizens' meeting? I'd like company, and you're good with paperwork.

Zainab

qa.q: How many visits has Zainab made to the tehsil office?
qa.a: Zainab has made four visits.

qa.q: How does Zainab feel about the delays, and what shows it?
qa.a: Zainab feels worn down and like "a number instead of a person", and was tempted to think nothing ever works, but chooses not to let cynicism win.

qa.q: What else could Zainab do to keep engaging with the problem?
qa.a: Keep the one-page guide updated, help more neighbours through the process, and back the petition for online tracking.

qa.q: How might the two neighbours have seen Zainab's one-page guide?
qa.a: As real help, since each of them finished in one visit instead of returning again and again.

grounding: Repeated delays leave Zainab feeling like a number, but Zainab chooses engagement by writing a guide for others and supporting reform.

The line outside the block office in the small town began at eight. Tanuja had brought a flask of tea and a packet of murukku. Beside her Zeenat, a stranger holding a thin folder, checked the phone for the fifth time.

"The clerk asked the man ahead of me for a ration card copy," Tanuja said quietly.

"I don't have one!"

"There's a copy shop across the road. Go, I'll keep your place."

Zeenat ran off and returned, out of breath. Tanuja passed over a cup of tea. The old man behind them explained that the second window shuts at one. Someone spread a newspaper on the ground to sit on. By noon the queue felt like a small gathering, everyone swapping tips and murukku.

Before the window opened, Tanuja wrote a number on Zeenat's folder. "Tell me how it goes."

qa.q: Where did Tanuja tell Zeenat to get a photocopy?
qa.a: Tanuja said there was a copy shop across the road.

qa.q: Why did Tanuja offer to keep Zeenat's place in the line?
qa.a: Tanuja saw a stranger who was worried and missing a copy, and shared stuckness made Tanuja want to ease things for someone in the same situation.

qa.q: How could people stuck in a slow queue make the wait easier for each other?
qa.a: Share tips about documents and windows, keep each other's places, pass around tea and snacks, and swap numbers to check in afterwards.

qa.q: How might Zeenat have felt when offered a place in the line?
qa.a: Zeenat, worried about the missing copy, may have felt relieved and less alone in a slow system.

grounding: Stuck in a long line, Tanuja shares tips, tea and snacks with a stranger and the queue becomes a small community.

passage:
Looking back, I expected the worst. My laptop bag had been stolen from a café near the bus stand, and I walked into the police station rehearsing an apology for wasting their time.

The officer at the desk, Sub-Inspector Anirban, offered me water and asked me to sit. He listened to the whole story without interrupting. I told him I had left the bag on the chair while I went to the counter. I almost skipped that part, but I told it straight. "That helps me," he said. "Now, what exactly was in the bag?"

He wrote the list with me, handed me a copy of the report, and added his number. A week later I called and he told me where the case stood. Nothing was recovered, but I had been treated like a person. I wrote him a thank-you note, and he pinned it on the board.

Dolma

qa.q: What did Dolma admit to the officer about the bag?
qa.a: Dolma admitted leaving the bag on the chair while going to the counter.

qa.q: What was Dolma expecting when walking into the police station?
qa.a: Dolma expected the worst and was rehearsing an apology for wasting their time, which shows a fear of being dismissed.

qa.q: What should someone do after reporting a theft?
qa.a: Cooperate honestly, keep the copy of the report, follow up by phone, and thank helpful officers, as Dolma did.

qa.q: How might Sub-Inspector Anirban have seen Dolma's honesty about the chair?
qa.a: As useful information: Anirban said "That helps me" and could then ask the right next questions.

grounding: A decent officer helps Dolma report a theft respectfully; Dolma cooperates honestly, follows up and thanks the officer.

passage:
Session note, Avni, campus career counsellor.

Jomon, aged 24, asked to see me after a friend posted a photo beside a new car, with screenshots of trading profits. Jomon said, "Everyone my age is ahead." Sleep had been poor for a week, and a trading account had been opened the night before but not yet funded.

I asked what the friend's posts leave out. Jomon thought for a while: losses, months of waiting, maybe borrowed money. I asked Jomon to write down a plan for the next year: savings, a certification, a small emergency fund. Jomon looked at the list and said, "It looks slow next to a car." I said slow is allowed.

Jomon agreed to read about how such accounts work before putting in any money. We meet again next month.

qa.q: What did the friend post that upset Jomon?
qa.a: The friend posted a photo beside a new car, with screenshots of trading profits.

qa.q: What does Jomon's remark "Everyone my age is ahead" suggest about Jomon's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Jomon feels left behind and envious, and the poor sleep for a week points to how much it weighs.

qa.q: What small step would help Jomon compare fairly?
qa.a: Compare against the written plan of savings, a certification and an emergency fund, and learn how trading accounts work before putting in money.

qa.q: How might the friend see those posts?
qa.a: The friend may simply be sharing a win without thinking how it lands on Jomon, and the posts leave out losses and waiting that Jomon guessed at.

grounding: A friend flaunts trading profits and Jomon feels left behind; the counsellor helps Jomon compare with their own plan instead of highlights.

Bidisha watched the video twice on the bus home. The finfluencer, smiling beside a beach, promised freedom in six months for anyone who followed the method. Bidisha had just seven thousand rupees left from her first salary savings. The number felt small, but the promise felt big, and her chest was fizzing.

She was about to tap "join the course" when Lakshmi, her flatmate, glanced at the screen.

"How does the finfluencer earn?"

"Um. Investing."

"Check."

Bidisha scrolled: course fees, referral codes at the bottom, a tiny line saying "not a registered adviser".

"And if it goes wrong?" Lakshmi asked.

Bidisha stared. The video hadn't answered that. She closed the tab, a little deflated, still liking the ambition. "I'll ask a registered adviser first."

qa.q: What did Bidisha find at the bottom of the page?
qa.a: Bidisha found referral codes and a tiny line saying "not a registered adviser".

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling before Lakshmi asked the questions?
qa.a: Bidisha felt inspired and excited, her chest fizzing, and was about to tap "join the course" on the strength of the promise.

qa.q: What could Bidisha do next before putting any money in?
qa.a: Ask a registered adviser, and find out how the finfluencer earns and what happens if the method goes wrong.

qa.q: How does Lakshmi see the finfluencer's video?
qa.a: Lakshmi treats it as something to be checked, asking how the finfluencer earns and what happens if it goes wrong.

grounding: Bidisha admires a finfluencer's promise but, prompted to verify how the finfluencer earns and what happens when it goes wrong, pauses to consult a registered adviser.

The channel message arrived at eleven at night: "Only 12 spots left. Doors close in 20 minutes." Below it a red countdown ticked, above a stack of screenshots showing profits in green. Usha's phone was at nine per cent, and her savings page sat open in another tab. Her pulse ran fast. Everyone in the group kept replying "Joined!"

Her cousin Imran, lying on the mattress across the room, stirred. "Why are you up?"

She showed him. He read for a while. "Twenty minutes to decide about money you worked for? Who decides like that?"

Usha noticed how tight her shoulders were. "The timer is doing the deciding."

"Sleep on it. Tomorrow show it to a registered adviser."

She put the phone face down on the charger. The timer ran out. Nothing terrible happened.

qa.q: How many spots did the message say were left?
qa.a: The message said only 12 spots were left.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling as the countdown ran, and what shows it?
qa.a: Usha felt pressured and anxious about missing out; the fast pulse and tight shoulders show it, along with the group replying "Joined!"

qa.q: What small step helped Usha take back control?
qa.a: Putting the phone face down, sleeping on it, and planning to show a registered adviser the next day.

qa.q: How does Imran see the twenty-minute deadline?
qa.a: Imran sees it as an odd way to decide about hard-earned money, and points out that the timer, not Usha, is making the decision.

grounding: Countdown timers, profit screenshots and fear of missing out pressure Usha, who notices the pressure, slows down and plans to check with a registered adviser.

passage:
Mahima refreshed the trading screen behind the counter of her uncle's hardware shop. Last week a tip had turned a small stake into three thousand. The thrill had hummed in her fingers all day, so the next stake was bigger. Then came a loss. Then a bigger stake "to get it back".

Sharmila, a friend from school who had come in for a packet of screws, noticed the phone tucked under the counter. "You've been on that since I arrived."

"It's just a small thing."

"Bigger bets after every win, and after every loss too?"

Mahima opened her mouth, then closed it. That was exactly what she had been doing.

That evening she wrote a limit in her notebook and moved the rest of her money back to her savings account, keeping some aside for emergencies. "Boring," she told Sharmila the next day. "But I can sleep."

qa.q: How much had the small stake turned into last week?
qa.a: The small stake had turned into three thousand.

qa.q: What did Mahima realise when Sharmila described the pattern?
qa.a: Mahima realised Sharmila had described exactly what she was doing: bigger bets after wins and bigger ones after losses to get the money back.

qa.q: What could Mahima do to avoid repeating the pattern?
qa.a: Keep the written limit, leave the rest in the savings account with some aside for emergencies, and talk to a qualified adviser if the urge returns.

qa.q: How does Sharmila see Mahima's trading?
qa.a: Sharmila notices the phone tucked under the counter and the pattern of ever-bigger bets, and raises it plainly but without a lecture.

grounding: Mahima's thrill at quick gains grows into bigger bets after wins and chasing losses; she notices the pattern, sets a limit and keeps savings.
